papers.text_quality: good (about 2,400 words; the whole short article including references; some accented characters garbled, nothing relevant lost)
papers.relied_on: Row 2 D4 assumed that the exogenous-insulin pattern needs an insulin assay that detects the analogue in use, and that reviews advise two assays with different cross-reactivity.
papers.full_text_shows: A short narrative review plus one adapted case report. The Roche Elecsys assay mostly detects human insulin and the glargine M1 metabolite and misses lispro, aspart, glulisine, detemir and degludec, while Access, Advia Centaur and Immulite show some cross-reactivity with lispro, aspart and glargine. The authors state that knowledge rests on case reports with no guideline or consensus, and advise two methods with different cross-reactivity early, then LC-MS/HRMS where available.
papers.quote: no single routinely used method is capable of detecting every insulin analog
papers.key_numbers: Pooled case reports cited from other papers: 31 adults (17 insulin-treated diabetes) and 40 children and adolescents. Index case: 20-year-old woman, aspart; Elecsys insulin low, insulin/C-peptide ratio always below 1, Immulite elevated, LC-MS/HRMS found aspart. No sensitivity or specificity given.
papers.role_in_work: Supports the availability and assay-knowledge point in row 2 D4 (and the row 2 caveat that some assays miss analogues).
papers.design: Narrative mini-review with one illustrative case report (adapted from Lotierzo 2022); expert opinion, no systematic search.
papers.population_and_size: One case; pooled case reports cited from other sources (31 adults, 40 children and adolescents).
papers.measure_type: Random insulin and C-peptide taken during spontaneous hypoglycaemia (insulin/C-peptide ratio); not a post-meal or stimulated test.
papers.assay_or_platform: Roche Elecsys (cobas 8000 e602), Siemens Immulite 2000 Xpi, LC-MS/HRMS for analogue identification; Beckman Access, Advia Centaur and Diasorin Liaison cross-reactivity from cited papers.
papers.quality_note: Low evidence level by the authors' own statement; no competing interest declared; 'emerging trend' is not a guideline. It does not give the Atellica or LC-MS/MS recovery figures that the D4 reason quotes (those come from other cited papers).

papers.text_quality: good (about 6,800 words; two-column layout interleaves lines; tables and supplementary figures not in the text)
papers.relied_on: Row 32 D7 used a pooled 35% of adults with DKA or ketosis at diabetes onset having ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes, described as 11 studies, n=2010.
papers.full_text_shows: The 35% (95% CI 24-49%, I2 94%) comes from 10 studies and 1,054 patients with ketosis or DKA at onset (400 with ketosis-prone type 2). The 2,010 patients (11 studies) belong to a second analysis of DKA regardless of timing, where prevalence was 25% (95% CI 14-42%, I2 97%). Studies were mostly Asian and African; one Caucasian study and one US study (mainly African-American and Hispanic patients); no age restriction was applied, so children were included.
papers.quote: Ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes accounts for one third of DKA or ketosis at the onset of diabetes in adults.
papers.key_numbers: 35% (24-49%), 10 studies, 1,054 patients, 400 cases; 25% (14-42%), 11 studies, 2,010 patients (any timing); I2 94% and 97%. Age MD 11.55 years (5.5-17.6), BMI MD 5.48 kg/m2 (3.25-7.72) versus type 1. Definition: ketosis, no islet autoantibodies, fasting and/or stimulated C-peptide within the reference range.
papers.role_in_work: Sole source for the ketosis-prone share in the row 32 D7 chain (patients with a non-classic DKA picture in whom type is in question).
papers.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42021283369), searched 15 Oct 2021 in five databases, random effects, JBI and QUIPS risk-of-bias tools; observational studies.
papers.population_and_size: 11 studies, 2,010 patients with DKA or ketosis, mainly Asian and African settings; includes children; excludes studies without C-peptide or autoantibody data.
papers.measure_type: C-peptide (fasting and/or stimulated) as part of the case definition, with islet autoantibodies; used to define the subgroup, not tested as a decision tool.
papers.assay_or_platform: Not standardised; C-peptide judged against each study's reference range.
papers.quality_note: Very high heterogeneity; the authors list varied definitions of ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes among their limitations; the evidence for US adults is thin (one US study, one Caucasian study). No conflicts of interest declared. The row 32 D7 range (13,000 to 80,000) stays in bin 3 for most of its span; transferability to the US is the main uncertainty.

papers.text_quality: good (about 13,000 words; registry chapter with figure captions; two-column interleaving)
papers.relied_on: Row 10 D7 used about 821 adult transplants in 2024 (plus about 23 paediatric) as the new-recipient base, then assumed 50% of new recipients and 10-30% of the prevalent pool have a C-peptide-based graft classification in a year.
papers.full_text_shows: 821 adult pancreas transplants in 2024 (892 in 2023, an 8.0% fall); adults are 96.9% of recipients, which implies roughly 25 paediatric transplants (derived, not stated). The chapter contains no mention of C-peptide. Registry pancreas graft failure is defined by removal, re-registration, islet registration, death, or total insulin use of 0.5 units/kg/day or more for 90 consecutive days, so national follow-up is insulin-dose based. It gives no count of prevalent recipients with functioning grafts or of islet transplants (islet pancreata are excluded from the recovery figures).
papers.quote: the overall number of adult pancreas transplants in the United States decreased to 821, an 8.0% drop from the prior year
papers.key_numbers: 821 adult transplants 2024 (892 in 2023); SPK waitlist additions 1,661 (1,585 in 2023); transplant rate 30.1 per 100 patient-years; pancreas graft loss within 90 days 5.1% PAK, 17.6% PTA, 5.9% SPK; 1-year graft failure 16.7% PAK, 8.3% PTA, 9.4% SPK (2023 transplants); 10-year mortality 27.5%, 13.1%, 20.6%.
papers.role_in_work: Source of the new-transplant count in the row 10 D7 chain; the unsourced C-peptide-classification shares and the prevalent pool are neither supported nor contradicted by it.
papers.design: National registry annual data report (descriptive, no inferential analysis).
papers.population_and_size: US adult pancreas transplant candidates and recipients, 2024 (821 transplants; 111 centres).
papers.measure_type: None; no insulin or C-peptide test is reported. Graft failure uses a total insulin dose criterion (non-test surrogate).
papers.quality_note: Reliable for transplant volumes. It cannot support any share of recipients receiving C-peptide testing; the OPTN definition suggests routine national graft classification does not use C-peptide, which is a reason to keep D7 confidence low, not to change the bin.

proposals.reason: The full text agrees with the D4 reasoning: assays differ in analogue detection, two assays are advised, LC-MS/HRMS is a send-out. Nothing in it moves availability by a point.
proposals.quote: no single routinely used method is capable of detecting every insulin analog

proposals.reason: The pooled 35% is real but belongs to 10 studies and 1,054 patients, mostly Asian and African. Using the 25% any-timing figure would leave the point estimate near the bin 3 boundary at the low end; the bin is decided mainly by the DKA count. Keep 3; confidence could be lowered to low-medium because of transferability.
proposals.quote: Ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes accounts for one third of DKA or ketosis at the onset of diabetes in adults.

proposals.reason: The 821 adult transplants is confirmed, but the paper gives no basis for the C-peptide share, and its graft-failure definition uses insulin dose, not C-peptide. The point estimate of about 2,000 (range 600 to 5,000) already rests on an assumption at low confidence. The paper alone would not move the score.
proposals.quote: the overall number of adult pancreas transplants in the United States decreased to 821, an 8.0% drop from the prior year

claim_issues.issue: States the 35% ketosis-prone share as '11 studies, n=2010'. In the paper the 35% is from 10 studies and 1,054 patients; 11 studies and 2,010 patients belong to the any-timing DKA analysis, where prevalence is 25%. The paper also does not restrict to adults.
claim_issues.proposed_wording: Meta-analysis (10 studies, 1,054 patients with DKA or ketosis at diabetes onset): pooled prevalence of ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes 35% (95% CI 24-49%, I2 94%); 25% (14-42%) across 11 studies and 2,010 patients with DKA regardless of timing. Studies were mainly Asian and African, and children were not excluded.

claim_issues.issue: The 'about 23 paediatric' figure is not stated in the OPTN/SRTR 2024 chapter, which says adults are 96.9% of recipients (about 25 paediatric by calculation). The chapter gives 892 adult transplants for 2023; the 915 figure comes from the 2023 report and was not checked here.
claim_issues.proposed_wording: 821 adult pancreas transplants in 2024 (892 in 2023); adults are 96.9% of recipients in 2024, so roughly 25 paediatric transplants (derived). Prevalent-pool and C-peptide-classification shares are assumptions and are not given in the report.

notes: No proposal changes a score. Current scores were read from V10.json (row 2 D4 = 2) and V1.json (row 32 D7 = 3; row 10 D7 = 2); I did not check whether a later unit supersedes them. A grep found none of the three PMIDs in claims/claims.csv or merged-conclusion.md. C276 is under 3,000 words because the article itself is short (3 pages), not because extraction was cut. Row 10 path to viability: not affected; the OPTN graft-failure definition (insulin dose) shows national follow-up does not depend on C-peptide. The 'about 25 paediatric' figure is my calculation (821 / 0.969), not a reported number. Tool calls used: 11 before writing the files, 2 to write them, plus a JSON parse check.
